title: Cayley graphs are just group gossip
excerpt: A group plus a set of generators is secretly a graph where every vertex has the same view — and that symmetry is why the spectral machinery works.
text: Handed a group $G$ and a symmetric generating set $S$, you get a graph for free. \begin{ definition } — Cayley graph For a group $G$ and symmetric $S \subseteq G$ (so $s \in S \Rightarrow s^{-1} \in S$), the Cayley graph $\mathrm{Cay}(G,S)$ has vertex set $G$ and an edge $\{g,h\}$ whenever $g^{-1}h \in S$. The setup Adjacency is a one-liner: $A_{g,h} = 1 \iff g^{-1}h \in S$. Symmetry of $S$ makes the graph undirected and $|S|$-regular. Why every vertex looks the same Left-multiplication by $a \in G$ sends $g \mapsto ag$ and preserves adjacency, since $(ag)^{-1}(ah) = g^{-1}h$. So $G$ acts on its own Cayley graph by automorphisms, transitively. Stand on any vertex and the neighbourhood looks identical. That is the property every averaging argument quietly leans on. A tiny example Take $\mathbb{Z}_n$ with $S=\{\pm 1\}$ and you have drawn a cycle $C_n$: def adjacent(g, h, S, n): return (h - g) % n in S # additive group: g^{-1}h is h - g Where the spectrum comes in For abelian $G$ the eigenvalues are character sums, $\lambda_\chi = \sum_{s \in S}\chi(s)$, so you read the spectral gap straight off the generators — and the gap controls mixing and expansion.

title: a field guide to “w”, kusa, and 草
excerpt: Why a serious Japanese thread suddenly sprouts a lawn — a short genealogy of online laughter.
text: Japanese www is laughter: warai (笑), clipped to a single w and stacked for volume. A wall of wwww looks like blades of grass, so people started writing 草 — literally “grass” — to mean the same thing. Escalate to 大草原 (“vast grassland”) and you have hit full ROFL. So when a grim thread abruptly grows a lawn, now you know what is being planted.
